title: The Incarnation and the Humiliation of the Word
english: Through the good-will of God and the Father, we are enriched in our supernatural nature by being in Christ, who raised us up and seated us in the heavenly places (Psalm 8:4-6).
For because He, the Savior of us all, is seated, He surpasses the whole boast of human nature.
We have become rich through Christ's poverty, but only if we are superior to all creation, for it is through His humility that we are exalted.

Therefore, let man be diminished a little from the angels, having become such, so that he might honor the human nature and recover it again to its original state, in glory and honor, being crowned in it, even though he is a lord of glory as God.

Just as the transgression of Adam demonstrated the most dishonorable state, so shall we be glorified through the obedience of Christ on our behalf, He having set forth His own soul so that He might rule both over the dead and the living (Psalm 8:4-6).
How is Christ diminished from the angels, He who is worshiped among them? It is because He sat within the measures of humanity; having received a body destined to die, He willingly suffered in it.
Yet through Him, having abolished death and rendered corruption inactive, He is crowned with the highest glories, being incorruption and life.
As for the things of superiority, they belong to the angels, for they are better off outside of flesh and of death, it having happened in these things of the Son through His voluntary emptying.

But Christ, though briefly diminished from the angels because of the measure of humanity, is worshiped by them in the excellence of His divinity; He is established upon thrones, which those standing around Him always glorify, calling Him Lord by the powers.
That He might taste death above all by the grace of God (Hebrews 2:9).
For as I think, what it means to have 'tasted all' is clear, as it is written, 'That he might taste death above all by the grace of God' (Hebrews 2:9).
For having given His own body to death, and as if having fleshly tasted that which occurred, He lived again and has immediately trampled the power of death.

Therefore, the One said to be briefly diminished from the angels is the Word who is from God; He did not suffer this diminishment into His own nature, for He is always the same, possessing the same nature, unshakeable and unchangeable, yet He has endured this also through us in a human way.

For He was sustaining Himself, even though by nature He is God, according to the measures of humanity because of the divine economy, and this is part of the mystery according to Him, that it is most proper to marvel at.

So also the prophet Habakkuk said, 'Lord, I have heard the sound of your hearing and I was afraid, I understood your works and was astonished' (Habakkuk 3:2), for truly, what has happened is an ecstasy and a wonder beyond all.

But I do not know how some, not having understood the mystery correctly, vaunt themselves and desire to interpret what is written in the eighth psalm, specifically the verse 'What is man, that you remember him, or a son of man, that you visit him?' (Psalm 8:4).

Let us therefore observe what kind of man it is that causes one to be struck with wonder, marveling that the Only-begotten was indeed worthy to be remembered by him and to have performed an inspection, as it is written, 'What is man, that you remember him, or a son of man, that you visit him?' (Psalm 8:4).

He proceeds from this to argue most clearly, as if the following had never been said of any man, that the blessed Paul, speaking of his own person, applied the words of the Psalm, saying 'made a little lower than the angels' (Psalm 8:5), we see Jesus being crowned with 'glory and honor' through the passion of death.

Furthermore, by distinguishing between natures, they claim privately that the man born of the Holy Virgin is a man of a strange sort; regarding this, they say that David marvels that he was worthy of both remembrance and visitation, and that he was worthy also of a unique nature above nature, as one receiving benefit from the Divine Word.

But they have failed to understand, as it appears, that Christ Jesus is not a man in Himself, understood and spoken of among us in a common or private sense; rather, it is the Word from God who has become man, and in order that the expression of the concepts may be properly understood…
The prophet David says, 'You have made him a little lower than the angels, and crowned him with glory and honor' (Psalm 8:5), and 'You have put all things under his feet' (Psalm 8:6).

title: Divine Promise and Human Nature
english: As the world unfolds in the necessary world, the wonder of Christ's name becomes apparent, and it is worth considering the theory presented in the psalm that has been placed before us.

The prophet David knew that according to the true and divine promise, Christ would be born from the fruit of his loins, and God, existing by nature, would sit among us in due time, speaking in the eighth psalm and making words to him as to a human and also to God, recognizing the one God from both.
He says, 'Lord, our Lord, how wonderful is your name in all the earth, for your magnificence has been lifted up above the heavens' (Psalm 8:1).
For where or among whom is Christ not wondered at, or how has his magnificence not been lifted up above the heavens?

If it is true that in the name of Jesus Christ every knee bends and every tongue confesses that Jesus Christ is Lord to the glory of God the Father (Philippians 2:10-11), then it is clear that Christ's name is indeed wonderful and his magnificence has been lifted up above the heavens.

When Christ raised Lazarus from the dead, all were amazed, and as he sat on a donkey, children waved palm branches and cried out 'Hosanna to the son of David, blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord' (Matthew 21:9).
The others rebuked them, but Christ said, 'Have you not read that I will perfect praise from the mouth of infants and sucklings?' (Matthew 21:16).

This event shows that even though Christ is God by nature, he humbled himself to such an extent that he allowed himself to be led by the crowd, and Paul declares that he has been stripped of the former glory, saying he has been stripped of it.
The blessed David saw the reason for this emptying and understood that it was so that Christ might rescue us from corruption and sin and the tyrannical hands of the devil.
The mystery of the economy with flesh is worthy of all wonder.
He says, 'Lord, what is man that you remember him, or the son of man that you visit him?' (Psalm 8:4).
For what is human nature in relation to God, and what is this that I say, what is human genus?
What portion is assigned to them on earth in relation to the orders of holy angels?
Even if man is nothing by nature and number, the Creator did not despise us, for he remembered us and deemed us worthy of visitation, as if we were perishing.

In the beginning, God brought us into existence, lowering us briefly below the angels, but then crowning us with honor and glory, setting us over the works of his hands, and subjecting all things under our feet.

The divine Paul skillfully sets forth the things concerning us, which have been renewed through Christ, and the scope of the whole song is in these things, appearing in the necessary world as it unfolds.
The things in Christ are a new creation, and the old things have passed away, and all things have become new.
The Holy Spirit says through one of the prophets, 'Take courage, Zion, do not let your hands weaken; the Lord your God is in you, to save you and renew you in his love' (Isaiah 41:10).
Paul declares us to be stripped of the former glory, and therefore, he says, 'Now we do not yet see all things subjected to him' (1 Corinthians 15:28).

title: Incarnation
english: Having sinned through Adam's transgression, humanity is shown to be in need of restoration, so that the one who enriches us may again be revealed. For the Word, being God by nature, humbled himself and became human, a little lower than the angels, to restore humanity to glory and honor. "We see Jesus, who was made a little lower than the angels, now crowned with glory and honor because he suffered death" (Hebrews 2:9).

If someone says that the man born of the Virgin is worthy of memory and care from God, they will bring shame, for where is Christ as a mere human, and when is he thought of without the united Word? How then can he be said to be worthy of care and memory from God?

The Lord is one, and our faith is one, and we have one baptism. Although the difference between natures is significant, the mode of union has revealed one Son from both. If we are worthy of memory from God the Word, then we are certainly psychic, lacking the spirit as it is written (1 Corinthians 14:14). We divide the one into two.

The body of the Word is not foreign to the Word itself. If the one born from the holy virgin has undergone emptying, how can he be emptied if he is glorified? Is it not an honor and glory for a human to be deemed worthy of oversight and memory, and to attain union with God? If they say that the emptying was done to the Monogenes, then he has been emptied by having suffered. For the one to whom suffering has happened, it is fitting that the matter of emptying has also happened.

Christ, as God, is deemed worthy of memory from God and has become one of the beneficiaries, and we approach Him as God in prayer, requesting the supply of heavenly goods, as He distributes the requests to all creation in a God-pleasing manner. This is evident because the children have shared in blood and flesh, and Christ has similarly shared in these things.

It is necessary to carefully examine which children the word is about, who have shared in flesh and blood, and how Christ has similarly participated in these things. When the Only-Begotten Word of God, being God and Lord by nature and co-throned with God the Father, was measured to the level of humanity, He was composed as a brother to those called through faith to the adoption of God. Then the economy's cleverness is well done.
